b: Fluid: substance that deforms continuously under any shear stress, however small.
Mass density (ρ): mass/volume. Water = 1000 kg/m³ at 4°C; air ≈ 1.225 kg/m³.
Dynamic viscosity (μ): unit N·s/m² = Pa·s; CGS unit poise (1 poise = 0.1 Pa·s). Water at 20°C ≈ 1 centipoise.
Kinematic viscosity (ν): ν = μ/ρ; unit m²/s; CGS unit stoke (1 stoke = 10⁻⁴ m²/s).
Temperature effect: viscosity of liquids decreases with temperature (cohesion falls); of gases increases (molecular momentum exchange rises).

Newtonian fluid: τ ∝ du/dy (water, air, oil). Non-Newtonian: dilatant (n > 1, e.g. quicksand), pseudoplastic (n < 1, e.g. blood, paint), Bingham plastic (yield stress, e.g. toothpaste, sewage sludge), thixotropic (printer ink).
Ideal fluid: incompressible and inviscid (μ = 0). Real fluid: has viscosity.
Bulk modulus K = −dp/(dV/V). Water ≈ 2.1 × 10⁹ N/m². Compressibility = 1/K.
Isothermal: K = p. Adiabatic: K = kp (k = 1.4 for air).
Surface tension (σ): force per unit length (N/m). Water–air at 20°C ≈ 0.073 N/m. Decreases with temperature.
Pressure inside droplet: Δp = 4σ/d. Soap bubble (two surfaces): Δp = 8σ/d. Liquid jet: Δp = 2σ/d.
Capillary rise: h = 4σ cosθ/(γd). Water–glass θ ≈ 0° (rise); mercury–glass θ ≈ 130–140° (depression).
Cohesion > adhesion → depression (mercury). Adhesion > cohesion → rise (water).
Vapour pressure: pressure at which liquid boils at given temperature; rises with temperature. Mercury has very low vapour pressure → used in barometers.
Cavitation: local pressure falls below vapour pressure → bubbles form and collapse → pitting of turbine runners, pump impellers.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

Non-Newtonian fluids: Pseudoplastic/shear-thinning (blood, paint, polymer solutions); dilatant/shear-thickening (sand-water, starch); Bingham plastic (toothpaste, sewage sludge, drilling mud — yield stress first); thixotropic (printer ink, some gels — viscosity falls with time).
Gas viscosity: Increases with temperature (molecular momentum transfer); liquid viscosity decreases (cohesion weakens).

b: Mass density ρ = m/V; water = 1000 kg/m³ (at 4 °C). Specific weight γ = ρg = 9.81 kN/m³ for water.
Specific gravity S = ρ/ρ(water at 4 °C). Mercury S = 13.6.
Viscosity of liquids decreases with temperature (cohesion falls); of gases increases (molecular momentum exchange rises).
Newtonian fluids: τ ∝ du/dy (water, air). Non-Newtonian: dilatant (shear thickening), pseudoplastic (shear thinning), Bingham plastic (yield stress, e.g. toothpaste, sewage sludge).
Ideal fluid: incompressible and zero viscosity.
Surface tension σ: unit N/m; water–air ≈ 0.073 N/m at 20 °C. Decreases with temperature.
Vapour pressure: pressure at which liquid boils; rises with temperature. Cavitation occurs when local pressure drops below vapour pressure.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Pascal's law: pressure at a point in a static fluid is equal in all directions.
Absolute = gauge + atmospheric. Vacuum pressure = atmospheric − absolute.
Standard atmosphere = 101.325 kPa = 760 mm Hg = 10.33 m of water.
Barometer: measures atmospheric pressure. Piezometer: simple gauge pressure; not for gases or high/negative pressure.
Simple U-tube manometer: gauge and vacuum pressure. Differential manometer: pressure difference between two points. Inverted U-tube: small differences with lighter fluid.
Micromanometer: very small pressure differences. Inclined manometer: improves sensitivity.
Bourdon gauge: mechanical; measures gauge pressure (high pressures).
Differential manometer reading (venturi, same liquid): h = x (S_m/S − 1).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Manometer rules: Move from one end to the other: add γh going down, subtract going up; in a U-tube differential manometer for same liquid in pipes: h = x(Sm/S − 1).
Inverted U-tube: Used for small pressure differences between two points of a liquid (lighter manometric fluid on top).
Pressure in units: 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa ≈ 10.2 m of water; 1 kg/cm² ≈ 98.1 kPa ≈ 10 m water.
Mercury: S = 13.6; 1 atm = 760 mm Hg = 10.33 m of water. Bourdon gauge reads gauge pressure.

s.t: More on this topic — Hydraulics: Fluid Pressure and Measurement
b: Absolute pressure = gauge pressure + atmospheric pressure. Vacuum = negative gauge pressure.
Piezometer: measures gauge pressure of liquids only; not for gases or negative pressure.
Simple U-tube manometer: measures positive and negative pressures.
Differential manometer: pressure difference between two points. Inverted U-tube for small differences.
Micromanometer / inclined manometer: very small pressure differences (higher sensitivity).
Mechanical gauges: Bourdon tube (most common), diaphragm, dead-weight gauge (used for calibration).
Barometer measures atmospheric pressure (mercury or aneroid).
Total pressure on plane surface: F = γ A h̄ (h̄ = depth of centroid).
Centre of pressure (vertical/inclined): h* = h̄ + I_G sin²θ/(A h̄). For vertical plane: h* = h̄ + I_G/(A h̄).
Centre of pressure always lies below centroid (except horizontal surface, where they coincide).
Vertical rectangle with top at free surface: h* = 2H/3 from surface.
Vertical triangle, apex at surface, base down: h* = 3H/4. Base at surface: h* = H/2.
Curved surface: horizontal component = force on vertical projection; vertical component = weight of liquid above (real or imaginary).
Lock gates: P = force on gate; reaction between gates R = P/(2 sin α).
Dam: resultant must lie in middle third to avoid tension.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. — Hydrostatic force on a vertical plane: pressure diagram, centroid G and centre of pressure P.
Given: Vertical rectangular gate 2 m wide × 3 m high, top edge 1 m below water surface.
Centre of pressure: I_G = 2 × 3³/12 = 4.5 m⁴; h* = 2.5 + 4.5/(6 × 2.5) = 2.8 m below the surface.
As depth of immersion increases, the centre of pressure moves closer to the centroid.

s.t: More on this topic — Hydraulics: Hydrostatic Forces on Surfaces
b: I_G: rectangle bd³/12; circle πd⁴/64; triangle bh³/36.
Applications: dams, lock gates, sluice gates, tank walls.
Archimedes' principle: buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced; acts at centre of buoyancy (centroid of displaced volume).
Metacentric height: GM = BM − BG, where BM = I/V (I = moment of inertia of waterline area about longitudinal axis).
Floating body: stable if M above G (GM > 0); neutral if GM = 0; unstable if M below G.
Time period of rolling: T = 2π √(k²/(g·GM)). Larger GM → more stable but uncomfortable (shorter period).
Typical GM: passenger ships 0.3–1.2 m (small for comfort); warships/cargo higher.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. — Stability of floating bodies: M above G (stable) and M below G (unstable).
Experimental GM: GM = w x / (W tan θ) — shift weight w by distance x, measure heel angle θ.
Large GM: Very stable but uncomfortable (quick rolling); small GM → slow rolling, comfortable — passenger ships keep small GM.
Floating body: stable if M above G. Fully submerged body (submarine, balloon): stable if B above G.

s.t: More on this topic — Hydraulics: Buoyancy and Floatation
b: Centre of buoyancy (B): centroid of displaced volume.
Metacentre (M): point where line of buoyant force of slightly tilted body cuts the original vertical axis.
Metacentric height GM = BM − BG, where BM = I/V (I = moment of inertia of waterplane area about tilting axis, V = displaced volume).
Submerged body stability: stable if B above G; neutral if coincide; unstable if B below G.
Time period of rolling T = 2π √(k² / (g·GM)). Larger GM → quicker, uncomfortable roll; passenger ships have small GM, warships larger GM.
Horizontal linear acceleration a: free surface slope tanθ = a/g.
Vertical acceleration a (upward): p = ρ h (g + a); downward: p = ρ h (g − a); free fall → p = 0.
Forced vortex (rotating container): paraboloid free surface, z = ω²r²/(2g). Velocity v = ωr.
Rise at wall = fall at centre (for cylinder initially at rest), each = ω²R²/(4g).
Free vortex: vr = constant; no external torque (e.g. whirlpool, flow in sink drain).
Steady flow: properties at a point do not change with time (∂/∂t = 0). Uniform flow: no change with distance (∂/∂s = 0).
Laminar vs turbulent; rotational vs irrotational; compressible vs incompressible; 1-D, 2-D, 3-D flow.
Streamline: tangent gives velocity direction; no flow across it. Pathline: path of one particle. Streakline: locus of particles passing through a point (dye).
Steady flow: streamline, pathline and streakline coincide.
Continuity (1-D, incompressible): Q = A₁V₁ = A₂V₂. General: ρ₁A₁V₁ = ρ₂A₂V₂.
Acceleration = local (∂V/∂t) + convective (V·∂V/∂s). Convective exists in steady non-uniform flow.
Rotation ωz = ½(∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y). Vorticity = 2ω. Irrotational if ω = 0.
Velocity potential (φ): u = −∂φ/∂x, v = −∂φ/∂y; exists only for irrotational flow; satisfies Laplace equation.
Stream function (ψ): u = −∂ψ/∂y, v = ∂ψ/∂x (sign convention varies); exists for 2-D continuous flow; difference of ψ = discharge per unit width.
Equipotential lines and streamlines intersect orthogonally → flow net.
Flow net not valid for: rotational flow, near solid boundaries (viscous effects), separation zones.
Free vortex: V·r = constant, irrotational (whirlpool, flow into drain). Forced vortex: V = ωr, rotational (rotating cylinder, impeller).
Forced vortex: free surface is paraboloid; rise above centre z = ω²r²/(2g).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Checks: Flow possible if continuity satisfied (∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0); φ exists only if flow is irrotational; ψ exists for any 2-D incompressible flow.
Streak line: Locus of all particles that passed through a fixed point (dye injection).
Flow net uses: Seepage under dams and through earth dams, groundwater flow, flow around bodies.
Streamlines and equipotential lines are orthogonal; in steady flow streamline = pathline = streakline.

s.t: More on this topic — Hydraulics: Fluid Kinematics
b: Steady flow: properties at a point do not change with time (∂/∂t = 0). Unsteady: they do.
Uniform flow: velocity does not change with distance along flow (∂V/∂s = 0). Non-uniform: it does.
Laminar: fluid moves in layers. Turbulent: random mixing.
Rotational vs irrotational: irrotational if rotation (ω) = 0 everywhere.
Pathline: path traced by a particle over time. Streakline: locus of particles passing through a fixed point (dye/smoke).
In steady flow streamlines, pathlines and streaklines coincide.
Stream function ψ: u = −∂ψ/∂y, v = ∂ψ/∂x (sign conventions vary); exists for 2D continuous flow (rotational or not).
Euler's equation (along streamline): dp/ρ + V dV + g dz = 0.
Bernoulli assumptions: steady, incompressible, inviscid (no friction), irrotational, along streamline, no shaft work/heat.
Terms: pressure head, velocity (kinetic) head, datum (potential) head. Sum = total head.
Hydraulic gradient line (HGL) = p/γ + z. Energy gradient line (EGL) = HGL + V²/2g; EGL always above HGL by V²/2g.
Kinetic energy correction factor α: laminar pipe = 2.0; turbulent ≈ 1.03–1.1.
Momentum correction factor β: laminar pipe = 4/3; turbulent ≈ 1.01–1.05.
Force of jet on stationary flat plate (normal): F = ρaV². On moving plate: ρa(V − u)².
Series of moving flat plates (wheel): F = ρaV(V − u); max efficiency 50% at u = V/2.
Curved vane, jet deflected 180°: theoretical efficiency 100% at u = V/2.
Moment of momentum: torque = ρQ(V₂r₂ − V₁r₁) → basis of turbines, sprinklers.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Applications of Bernoulli: Venturimeter, orifice meter, pitot tube, flow from orifices, siphons, lift on aerofoils.
Jet on hinged/inclined plate: Force normal to inclined plate F = ρaV² sin θ.
Moving curved vane: Work done/s = ρaV(V − u)(1 + cos φ)u for symmetric vane — basis of Pelton wheel.
HGL lies below EGL by V²/2g; HGL can go below pipe centreline (negative pressure — siphon); EGL always slopes down in direction of flow.

s.t: More on this topic — Hydraulics: Fluid Dynamics
b: Euler equation (along streamline): dp/ρ + g dz + V dV = 0. Assumes ideal, steady flow.
Bernoulli's equation: p/ρg + V²/2g + z = constant (pressure head + velocity head + datum head).
Assumptions: steady, ideal (inviscid), incompressible, along a streamline, irrotational (for across streamlines).
Real fluid: p₁/ρg + V₁²/2g + z₁ = p₂/ρg + V₂²/2g + z₂ + h_L.
Kinetic energy correction factor α: laminar pipe flow = 2; turbulent ≈ 1.03–1.1.
Momentum correction factor β: laminar pipe flow = 4/3; turbulent ≈ 1.01–1.04.
Impulse–momentum equation: ΣF = ρQ(V₂ − V₁). Used for pipe bends, nozzles, jets.
Moment of momentum equation: basis of turbines, sprinklers, centrifugal pumps.
Jet on series of moving flat vanes: max efficiency 50% at u = V/2. Curved vanes (Pelton) max theoretical efficiency 100% at u = V/2 with 180° deflection.
Venturimeter: Q = Cd·a₁a₂√(2gh)/√(a₁² − a₂²). Cd ≈ 0.95–0.99. Convergent cone ~ 20–22°, divergent 5–7° (avoids separation).
Flow nozzle: Cd between venturi and orifice meter.
Pitot tube: measures point velocity, V = Cv√(2gh). Pitot-static tube measures stagnation − static.
Rotameter: variable-area meter. Current meter: velocity in open channels/rivers.
Orifice coefficients: Cd = Cc × Cv. Typical Cc ≈ 0.64, Cv ≈ 0.97–0.98, Cd ≈ 0.62.
Vena contracta: section of minimum jet area, about d/2 from orifice.
Small orifice: Q = Cd·a√(2gH). Large rectangular orifice: Q = ⅔ Cd b√(2g)(H₂^1.5 − H₁^1.5).
Time to empty tank (orifice at bottom): T = 2A(√H₁ − √H₂)/(Cd·a√(2g)).
Hemispherical tank emptying and other shapes — derive from A·dh = −Cd·a√(2gh)dt.
External cylindrical mouthpiece: Cd = 0.855. Convergent–divergent: Cd = 1.0. Borda's (re-entrant) running free: Cd = 0.5; running full: 0.707.
Rectangular notch/weir: Q = ⅔ Cd L√(2g) H^1.5.
Triangular (V) notch: Q = (8/15) Cd tan(θ/2)√(2g) H^2.5. 90° V-notch: Q ≈ 1.417 H^2.5 (Cd = 0.6). Best for low discharges; error in H affects Q more (2.5 × %).
Error in Q from error in H: rectangular dQ/Q = 1.5 dH/H; triangular = 2.5 dH/H.
Trapezoidal (Cipolletti) weir: side slopes 1H:4V; compensates end contractions.
Francis formula: Q = 1.84 (L − 0.1nH) H^1.5 (n = number of end contractions).
Broad-crested weir: Q_max = 1.705 Cd L H^1.5 (critical depth = ⅔H).
Ogee weir: profile follows lower nappe of sharp-crested weir; used as dam spillway.
Velocity of approach increases discharge; Bazin and Rehbock formulas account for it.
Submerged (drowned) weir: treated as free weir + drowned orifice.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. — Venturimeter: converging cone, throat and long diverging cone; piezometric difference h.
Inclined venturimeter: Reading of differential manometer is independent of the inclination; Q depends only on manometer reading.
Orifice meter: Orifice dia ≈ 0.5 D; Cd ≈ 0.6–0.65; vena contracta ≈ 0.5 D downstream.
Cd order: venturimeter (0.95–0.98) > flow nozzle (0.93–0.98) > orifice meter (0.6–0.65). Head loss order is the reverse.
Classification: By size (small/large), shape (circular, rectangular, triangular), edge (sharp/bell-mouthed), discharge (free/drowned/partially submerged).
Time to empty: T = 2A(√H₁ − √H₂)/(Cd a √(2g)); for full emptying H₂ = 0.
Mouthpiece types: External cylindrical (Cd 0.855), convergent (Cd ≈ 0.975), convergent-divergent (highest), Borda/re-entrant (0.5 free, 0.707 full).
Fig. — Rectangular, triangular (V) and Cipolletti notches with discharge formulas.
Error sensitivity: dQ/Q = 1.5 dH/H (rectangular); 2.5 dH/H (triangular) — V-notch needs more precise head measurement.
Why V-notch: Same Cd over wide range of heads; accurate for small discharges; only one parameter (θ).
End contractions (Francis): Effective length L − 0.1nH (n = number of end contractions).
Cipolletti weir side slopes 1 H : 4 V compensate for end contractions → Q = 1.86 L H^(3/2).

s.t: More on this topic — Hydraulics: Flow Measurement
b: Venturimeter: Q = C_d A₁A₂ √(2gh) / √(A₁² − A₂²). C_d ≈ 0.95–0.98. Convergent cone ≈ 20–22°, divergent 5–7° (long, to avoid separation). Throat diameter ≈ 1/3 to 3/4 of pipe diameter.
Orifice meter: cheaper, compact, higher head loss; C_d ≈ 0.6–0.65.
Pitot-static (Prandtl) tube: stagnation minus static pressure → velocity.
Rotameter: variable-area meter; float position indicates flow rate.
Current meter: velocity in rivers/open channels.
Hot-wire anemometer: velocity fluctuations in turbulent flow (gases).
Head loss order (highest → lowest): orifice meter > flow nozzle > venturimeter.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

s.t: More on this topic — Hydraulics: Orifices and Mouthpieces
b: C_c = jet area at vena contracta / orifice area ≈ 0.61–0.69.
C_v from jet trajectory: C_v = x / √(4yH).
Large rectangular orifice: Q = (2/3) C_d b √(2g) (H₂^1.5 − H₁^1.5).
External cylindrical mouthpiece: C_d ≈ 0.855; requires length ≈ 3d; vacuum at vena contracta ≈ 0.89H.
Convergent–divergent mouthpiece: highest C_d (≈ 1.0 based on throat).
Borda (internal/re-entrant) mouthpiece: running free C_d = 0.5; running full C_d ≈ 0.707.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

s.t: More on this topic — Hydraulics: Notches and Weirs
b: Notch: small opening in tank side; weir: larger structure across river/channel.
Triangular (V-notch): Q = (8/15) C_d tan(θ/2) √(2g) H^2.5. For 90°: Q ≈ 1.417 H^2.5 (C_d = 0.6). Most accurate for low flows.
Cipolletti weir: trapezoidal with side slopes 1H:4V (14°); slope compensates end contractions. Q = 1.86 L H^1.5.
Francis' formula (end contractions): L_eff = L − 0.1nH (n = number of end contractions).
Broad-crested weir: Q_max = 1.705 C_d L H^1.5 (critical depth = 2H/3 on crest).
Ogee weir: crest shaped to lower nappe profile; used as dam spillway.
Submerged weir: downstream water above crest; treat as free part + drowned part.
Velocity of approach increases discharge; include head ha = Va²/2g.
Error in discharge due to error in head: rectangular dQ/Q = 1.5 dH/H; triangular dQ/Q = 2.5 dH/H.
Ventilation of weir required to keep nappe free (prevent pressure drop under nappe).
Fundamental dimensions: M, L, T. Force = MLT⁻². Viscosity μ = ML⁻¹T⁻¹. ν = L²T⁻¹. Surface tension = MT⁻². Power = ML²T⁻³.
Rayleigh's method: suitable for up to 3–4 variables.
Buckingham π theorem: n variables, m fundamental dimensions → (n − m) π terms. Repeating variables must not form a π term themselves and should include geometry, flow and fluid property.
Reynolds number Re = ρVL/μ = inertia/viscous. Model law for pipe flow, submarines, aircraft (subsonic), flow around fully submerged bodies.
Froude number Fr = V/√(gL) = inertia/gravity. Model law for open channels, spillways, weirs, ships, waves, hydraulic jump.
Weber number We = V/√(σ/ρL) = inertia/surface tension. Capillary flows, droplets, very shallow flows.
Mach number M = V/C = inertia/elastic. Compressible flows, aircraft at high speed. M < 1 subsonic, = 1 sonic, > 1 supersonic, > 5 hypersonic.
Euler number Eu = V/√(p/ρ) = inertia/pressure. Cavitation, pressure-dominated flow.
Froude model scale ratios (Lr): Vr = Lr^½, Tr = Lr^½, Qr = Lr^2.5, Fr (force) = Lr³, Pr (power) = Lr^3.5.
Distorted models: different horizontal and vertical scales; used for rivers and harbours.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Pipe flow, submarines, aircraft at low speed, flow meters
Spillways, open channels, ships (wave resistance), weirs, river models
Froude model example: Spillway model 1:25; prototype Q = Qm × Lr^2.5 = Qm × 3125.
Froude scale ratios: Vr = Lr^½, Qr = Lr^(5/2), Tr = Lr^½, Fr(force) = Lr³, Pr(power) = Lr^(7/2).

s.t: More on this topic — Hydraulics: Dimensional Analysis and Similitude
b: Fundamental dimensions: M, L, T (and θ for temperature).
Rayleigh's method: suits ≤ 4 variables. Buckingham π theorem: n variables, m fundamental dimensions → (n − m) π terms.
Repeating variables: should not form a π term by themselves; usually one geometric, one flow, one fluid property (e.g. D, V, ρ).
Reynolds number (inertia/viscous): pipe flow, submarines, aircraft at low speed, flow meters.
Euler number (pressure/inertia): flow with pressure dominance, cavitation studies.
Froude model laws (scale ratio Lr): Vr = Lr^0.5, Qr = Lr^2.5, Tr = Lr^0.5, Fr(force) = Lr³, Pr(power) = Lr^3.5.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Pipe flow: laminar Re < 2000; transition 2000–4000; turbulent > 4000. Open channel (Re based on R): laminar < 500, turbulent > 2000 (approx.).
Shear stress varies linearly: zero at centre, maximum at wall.
Between fixed parallel plates: Vmax = 1.5 Vavg; hf = 12μVL/(γB²).
Couette flow: one plate moving, linear velocity profile (no pressure gradient).
Stokes' law (sphere, Re < 1): Drag F = 3πμDV; Cd = 24/Re. Terminal velocity V = D²(γs − γ)/(18μ) → falling-sphere viscometer, settling of particles.
Dashpot, capillary tube viscometer (Poiseuille), rotating cylinder viscometer.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. — Velocity distribution in pipes: laminar (parabolic) and turbulent (flatter).
Hagen–Poiseuille: Q = πD⁴Δp/(128μL); head loss ∝ V (laminar) but ∝ V² (turbulent).
Power to overcome viscous resistance: In a journal bearing P ∝ μ N² D³ L / t.
Laminar: f = 64/Re, Vmax = 2 Vavg, α = 2, β = 4/3. Between parallel plates: Vmax = 1.5 Vavg.

s.t: More on this topic — Hydraulics: Laminar Flow
b: Reynolds number Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν (ratio of inertia to viscous forces).
Open channel (Re based on hydraulic radius R): laminar < 500, turbulent > 2000 (approx.).
Hagen–Poiseuille (circular pipe): h_f = 32 μ V L / (ρ g D²).
Viscometers: capillary tube, falling sphere, rotating cylinder, orifice type (Saybolt, Redwood).

chapters.t: Turbulent Flow and Flow Through Pipes
b: Darcy–Weisbach: hf = fLV²/(2gD) = fLQ²/(12.1 D⁵). Loss ∝ V² (fully turbulent); ∝ Q²/D⁵.
Chezy: V = C√(RS). Relation C = √(8g/f). Manning: V = (1/n) R^⅔ S^½. Hazen–Williams: V = 0.849 C R^0.63 S^0.54 (SI).
Hydraulic mean depth R = A/P. Pipe flowing full: R = D/4.
Hydraulically smooth: roughness k < laminar sublayer δ′; rough: k > 6δ′ (f independent of Re).
Laminar sublayer thickness δ′ = 11.6ν/V*. Shear velocity V* = √(τ₀/ρ).
Turbulent velocity profile: logarithmic (Prandtl). Vmax ≈ 1.2–1.25 Vavg; shear stress = laminar + turbulent (Reynolds stress).
Prandtl mixing length theory; eddy viscosity.
Moody diagram: f vs Re and relative roughness k/D; Colebrook–White equation.
Sudden contraction: hL = (1/Cc − 1)² V₂²/2g with Cc = 0.62 this gives ≈ 0.375 V₂²/2g; taken as 0.5 V₂²/2g when Cc is not given.
Entrance loss = 0.5 V²/2g; exit loss = V²/2g; bend/fitting loss = kV²/2g.
Pipes in series: Q same; losses add. Equivalent pipe (Dupuit): L/D⁵ = ΣLi/Di⁵.
Pipes in parallel: head loss same; discharges add.
Power transmission through pipe: P = γQ(H − hf). Maximum when hf = H/3 → max efficiency 66.7%.
Nozzle at end of pipe: max power when head loss in pipe = H/3; optimum nozzle diameter d = (D⁵/(2fL))^¼ with Darcy f [= (D⁵/(8fL))^¼ if hf = 4fLV²/2gD is used].
Siphon: summit should not be more than about 7.6 m above the supply water level, to avoid vapour/air separation.
Water hammer: sudden valve closure → pressure rise. Rigid pipe: p = ρVC; time 2L/C (critical time). Rapid closure t < 2L/C. Slow closure: p = ρLV/t. Surge tank protects pipes.
Hardy Cross method: pipe network analysis (Σhf = 0 around loop; Σ Q = 0 at junction).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. — Moody diagram (computed from Colebrook–White): laminar line, transition, smooth and rough pipe curves.
Smooth pipe: f depends on Re only; fully rough: f depends on k/D only; transition zone: on both (Colebrook).
Siphon limit: Summit not more than ≈ 7.5–8 m above the HGL/inlet level (vapour pressure, dissolved air).
Three-reservoir problem: Solve by assuming the junction head; continuity at junction must balance.
Series: Q same, hf adds. Parallel: hf same, Q adds. Dupuit equivalent pipe: L/D⁵ = ΣLi/Di⁵.
Wave speed in elastic pipe: c = √[(K/ρ)/(1 + KD/(Et))] — thinner/elastic pipe walls reduce c and hence surge pressure.
Surge tank types: Simple, restricted-orifice, differential (Johnson), closed (air) surge tanks.
Rapid closure (t < 2L/c): pressure rise = ρcV (Joukowski) — independent of pipe length.

s.t: More on this topic — Hydraulics: Turbulent Flow and Boundary Layer
b: Turbulent shear: Boussinesq eddy viscosity; Prandtl mixing length theory τ = ρ l² (du/dy)².
Velocity profile is flatter (logarithmic); V_max ≈ 1.2 V_avg in pipes.
Colebrook–White equation and Moody diagram give f for commercial pipes.
In fully rough zone f depends only on relative roughness k/D, not Re.
Boundary layer: thin region near wall where velocity rises from 0 to 99% of free stream.
Laminar BL thickness (Blasius): δ = 5x / √Re_x. Turbulent: δ = 0.37x / Re_x^0.2.
Transition on flat plate at Re_x ≈ 5 × 10⁵.
Displacement thickness δ* > momentum thickness θ > energy thickness. Shape factor H = δ*/θ (laminar flat plate ≈ 2.59).
Separation occurs under adverse pressure gradient (dp/dx > 0) where (du/dy) at wall = 0.
Separation control: streamlining, suction, blowing, rotating cylinder, slots.
Drag = pressure (form) drag + friction (skin) drag. Lift via circulation (Kutta–Joukowski: L = ρVΓ per unit length). Magnus effect: rotating body in a stream.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Thickness relations (laminar, Blasius): δ = 5x/√Rex; δ* ≈ δ/3; θ ≈ δ/7.5; shape factor H = δ*/θ ≈ 2.6 (laminar), ≈ 1.3–1.4 (turbulent).
Turbulent BL: δ = 0.37x/Rex^(1/5); grows faster than laminar BL.
Separation occurs where ∂u/∂y = 0 at the wall (wall shear zero) under adverse pressure gradient.

s.t: More on this topic — Hydraulics: Flow Through Pipes
b: Darcy–Weisbach: h_f = f L V² / (2gD) (f = Darcy friction factor = 4 × Fanning f').
Chezy: V = C √(R S); Hazen–Williams: V = 0.849 C R^0.63 S^0.54 (water supply design).
Minor losses: sudden expansion h = (V₁ − V₂)²/2g (Borda–Carnot). Sudden contraction h = (1/C_c − 1)² V₂²/2g ≈ 0.5V²/2g at entry.
Equivalent length method: minor loss expressed as extra pipe length.
Siphon: pipe rising above hydraulic gradient; summit pressure must stay above vapour pressure (practical limit ≈ 7.6 m of water below atmosphere).
Nozzle at pipe end for maximum power: d = (D⁵ / (2fL))^0.25 with Darcy f [= (D⁵/(8fL))^0.25 if h_f = 4fLV²/2gD is used].
Pipe networks: Hardy Cross method (loop corrections ΔQ = −Σh / (n Σ h/Q)).
Branching pipes: three-reservoir problem — continuity at junction plus energy along each pipe.
Water hammer: pressure surge from sudden valve closure in pipe.
Wave velocity c = √(K/ρ) (rigid pipe); elastic pipe: c = √(K/ρ) / √(1 + KD/(Et)).
Critical time = 2L/c. Closure faster than this is "rapid".
Rapid closure (rigid pipe): pressure rise p = ρ c V (Joukowsky).
Gradual closure (t > 2L/c): p = ρ L V / t.
Protection: surge tank, slow-closing valves, relief valves, air chambers.
Surge tank located between reservoir and turbine/valve on penstock; types: simple, restricted orifice, differential.
Boundary layer: thin region near wall where velocity rises from 0 to 99% of free stream (Prandtl, 1904).
Displacement thickness δ*, momentum thickness θ, energy thickness δ**. Shape factor H = δ*/θ (laminar flat plate ≈ 2.6, turbulent ≈ 1.3–1.4).
Laminar boundary layer over flat plate (Blasius): δ = 5x/√Re_x. Turbulent: δ = 0.37x/Re_x^0.2.
Separation control: streamlining, suction, blowing, rotating cylinder, slotted wing, vortex generators.
Drag = pressure (form) drag + friction (skin) drag. Streamlined bodies: mainly friction drag; bluff bodies: mainly pressure drag.
F_D = ½ Cd ρ A V²; F_L = ½ CL ρ A V².
Golf ball dimples: trigger turbulent boundary layer → delayed separation → lower pressure drag.
Magnus effect: lift on rotating cylinder/sphere in flow (spin of balls).
Kutta–Joukowski: lift per unit span L = ρVΓ (Γ = circulation).
Drag crisis: sudden drop in Cd of sphere/cylinder at Re ≈ 2–5 × 10⁵.
Aerofoil stall: at high angle of attack flow separates → lift drops.
Free surface at atmospheric pressure; driving force is gravity.
Froude number Fr = V/√(gD) (D = hydraulic depth A/T). Fr < 1 subcritical (tranquil), = 1 critical, > 1 supercritical (rapid/shooting).
Specific energy E = y + V²/2g. Minimum specific energy at critical depth.
Rectangular channel: yc = (q²/g)^⅓; Emin = 1.5 yc; Vc = √(g yc).
Alternate depths: same E, different depths (sub and supercritical). Sequent (conjugate) depths: same specific force (before and after jump).
Most economical section (max Q for given A):
Trapezoidal: half regular hexagon; R = y/2; sloping side = half top width; side slope 60° to horizontal.
Circular (max velocity): y = 0.81D; (max discharge): y ≈ 0.938D (Manning; ≈ 0.95D with Chezy).
Hydraulic jump: supercritical to subcritical. Rectangular: y₂/y₁ = ½(−1 + √(1 + 8Fr₁²)).
Jump types (Fr₁): undular 1–1.7; weak 1.7–2.5; oscillating 2.5–4.5; steady 4.5–9 (best for energy dissipation); strong > 9.
Length of jump ≈ 5–7 (y₂ − y₁); commonly 6(y₂ − y₁).
Uses of jump: energy dissipation below spillways, mixing chemicals, raising water level, aeration.
Slopes: Mild (M) yn > yc; Steep (S) yn < yc; Critical (C) yn = yc; Horizontal (H) S₀ = 0; Adverse (A) S₀ < 0.
Surface profiles: M1 (backwater curve behind dam/weir), M2 (drawdown, approaching free fall), M3 (below sluice on mild slope); 12 profiles total (M1–3, S1–3, C1, C3, H2–3, A2–3).
Control section: where depth-discharge relation is fixed (e.g. critical depth at free overfall, ≈ 1.4 × brink depth: brink depth ≈ 0.715 yc).
Manning n typical: smooth concrete 0.012–0.013; earth channel 0.022–0.025; natural streams 0.03+.
Critical depth meter / venturi flume / Parshall flume used for discharge measurement in channels.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. — Specific energy curve: critical depth, alternate depths, subcritical and supercritical limbs.
Fig. — GVF profiles on a mild slope: M1 (backwater), M2 (drawdown) and M3 (below a sluice gate).
Given: Rectangular channel 4 m wide, Q = 12 m³/s → q = 3 m²/s.
Critical flow: Fr = 1, minimum specific energy for given Q, maximum Q for given E; rectangular: yc = ⅔ Ec.
Location: Below spillways, sluice gates and falls where supercritical flow meets subcritical tail water.
Efficiency of jump: E₂/E₁ — lower for stronger jumps; relative loss ΔE/E₁ rises with Fr₁.
Steady jump Fr₁ 4.5–9 (best for stilling basins); oscillating jump 2.5–4.5 should be avoided (waves).

s.t: More on this topic — Hydraulics: Open Channel Flow — Basics and Uniform Flow
b: Types: steady/unsteady; uniform/non-uniform (gradually varied GVF, rapidly varied RVF).
Hydraulic radius R = A/P (wetted perimeter). Hydraulic depth D = A/T (top width).
Chezy: V = C√(RS). Manning: V = (1/n) R^(2/3) S^(1/2) (SI). Relation C = R^(1/6)/n.
Bazin and Kutter formulae give Chezy C in terms of roughness.
Most economical (efficient) section: maximum Q for given A, i.e. minimum P.
Trapezoidal: half-regular hexagon; R = y/2; sloping sides tangent to semicircle centred on free surface; side slope 1V:√3H (60°) optimal.
Circular: max discharge at y ≈ 0.938D (Manning); max velocity at y ≈ 0.81D.
Normal depth y_n: depth at uniform flow.
Specific energy E = y + V²/2g (measured from channel bed).
Critical depth: minimum specific energy for a given discharge; Fr = 1.
Rectangular channel: y_c = (q²/g)^(1/3); E_min = 1.5 y_c; V_c = √(g y_c).
Alternate depths: two depths with same E for given q (one sub-, one supercritical).
Specific force (momentum function) M = Q²/(gA) + A z̄; conjugate (sequent) depths have equal M.
Critical slope S_c: slope giving normal depth = critical depth. Mild: y_n > y_c; steep: y_n < y_c.
Critical depth meters: venturi flume, Parshall flume, broad-crested weir (flow passes through critical depth).
Hump in subcritical flow: water surface drops; in supercritical: rises. Contraction in width: similar behaviour.
Sudden rise from supercritical to subcritical flow; large energy dissipation.
Energy loss: ΔE = (y₂ − y₁)³ / (4 y₁ y₂).
Length of jump ≈ 5 to 7 × (y₂ − y₁) (≈ 6.9(y₂ − y₁) commonly used).
Classification by Fr₁: undular 1–1.7; weak 1.7–2.5; oscillating 2.5–4.5; steady 4.5–9 (best for stilling basins); strong > 9.
Uses: energy dissipation below spillways/sluices, raising downstream water level, mixing chemicals, aeration, removing air pockets.
Jump is a rapidly varied flow (RVF); momentum (not energy) is conserved across it.
Assumptions: hydrostatic pressure, uniform-flow friction formula applies locally, small slope, constant n.
Slope classes: Mild (M), Steep (S), Critical (C), Horizontal (H), Adverse (A).
Zones: 1 = above both y_n and y_c; 2 = between them; 3 = below both.
M1 (backwater curve): upstream of dam/weir — most common.
M2 (drawdown curve): upstream of a free overfall/drop.
M3: downstream of sluice gate on mild slope (ends in jump).
S1: upstream of dam on steep slope (begins with jump). S2: downstream of slope change mild→steep. S3: below sluice on steep slope.
No H1 and A1 curves exist (normal depth infinite/undefined).
Computation: direct step method (prismatic channels), standard step method (natural channels), graphical integration.
Control sections: where depth–discharge relation is fixed (critical depth at free overfall, weirs, gates).
Impulse turbine (Pelton): high head (> 250 m), low discharge, tangential flow; jet at atmospheric pressure; no draft tube.
Pelton: max efficiency at bucket speed u = V/2; jet ratio m = D/d ≈ 12 (10–14); deflection ≈ 165°. Speed ratio ku ≈ 0.43–0.47.
Reaction turbines: Francis (medium head 60–250 m, mixed/radial-inward flow); Kaplan (low head < 60 m, high discharge, axial flow, adjustable blades); Propeller (fixed blades).
Degree of reaction: Pelton = 0; Francis ≈ 0.5–0.9; Kaplan high.
Draft tube: in reaction turbines; recovers kinetic energy and allows turbine above tailrace. Types: conical (efficiency ~90%), elbow, Moody spreading, simple elbow.
Specific speed Ns = N√P/H^(5/4) (P in metric horsepower; in SI with P in kW: Pelton 8.5–30, Francis 50–340, Kaplan 255–860):
Unit speed Nu = N/√H; unit discharge Qu = Q/√H; unit power Pu = P/H^1.5.
Hydraulic efficiency = runner power/water power; overall η = mechanical × hydraulic.
Governing: Pelton by spear (needle) valve and deflector; Francis by wicket (guide) gates; Kaplan by guide vanes + runner blades.
Thoma's cavitation factor σ = (Ha − Hv − Hs)/H; used to fix turbine setting above tail water.
Surge tank: protects penstock from water hammer.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. — Choice of turbine by specific speed and head.

Pakistan hydropower: Tarbela & Mangla — Francis turbines; Ghazi Barotha (Indus, run-of-river channel) — Francis; Neelum–Jhelum (969 MW) — Francis; high-head small hydel in KP/GB often Pelton; low-head canal-fall hydel — Kaplan/bulb units.
Draft tube types: Conical (efficiency ≈ 90%), simple elbow, elbow with varying cross-section, Moody spreading tube.
Pelton: tangential, impulse, high head, low Ns, degree of reaction 0; Kaplan: axial, adjustable blades, low head, high Ns.

s.t: More on this topic — Hydraulics: Impact of Jets and Hydraulic Turbines
b: Turbine converts hydraulic energy into mechanical energy.
Impulse turbine (Pelton wheel): all available head converted to kinetic energy in nozzle; runs at atmospheric pressure; high head (> 250 m), low discharge.
Reaction turbines: part pressure, part kinetic; runner full of water; draft tube required.
Francis: mixed/radial inward flow; medium head (≈ 30–250 m).
Kaplan: axial flow, adjustable runner blades; low head (< 30 m), high discharge. Propeller turbine: fixed blades.
Pelton: jet ratio m = D/d ≈ 12 (min 6); bucket speed ratio u/V ≈ 0.46; bucket deflection ≈ 165°; number of buckets ≈ 15 + D/(2d).
Specific speed N_s = N√P / H^(5/4). Pelton (single jet) ≈ 8.5–30; Francis ≈ 50–340; Kaplan ≈ 255–860 (SI, P in kW).
Efficiencies: hydraulic, mechanical, volumetric; overall = mechanical × hydraulic (× volumetric).
Unit quantities (unit speed, unit discharge, unit power) predict performance at different heads.
Draft tube: recovers kinetic energy at exit, allows turbine above tail race; types — conical (most efficient, ≈ 90%), elbow, Moody spreading.
Cavitation in turbines: assessed by Thoma cavitation factor σ; most likely at runner exit (reaction turbines).
Governing of turbines: speed kept constant by adjusting flow (spear valve in Pelton, guide vanes in Francis/Kaplan).
Penstock: pipe carrying water from reservoir to turbine.
Centrifugal pump: converts mechanical energy to pressure energy via centrifugal action; casing types: volute, vortex, diffuser (turbine pump).
Priming: required before starting centrifugal pump (fill casing and suction pipe with liquid).
Manometric head Hm = Hs + Hd + losses + Vd²/2g. Manometric efficiency = gHm/(Vw₂u₂).
Minimum starting speed: N = 120 ηman Vw₂D₂/(π(D₂² − D₁²)).
Specific speed of pump Ns = N√Q/H^(3/4).
Low Ns → radial flow (high head); high Ns → axial flow (low head, high Q).
Pumps in series → increase head; in parallel → increase discharge.
Backward-curved vanes: most common, stable characteristic, non-overloading.
Affinity laws: Q ∝ ND³, H ∝ N²D², P ∝ N³D⁵.
NPSH available must exceed NPSH required to avoid cavitation.
Reciprocating pump: positive displacement; for small Q, high head; no priming needed.
Slip = Q_th − Q_act. Negative slip when delivery pipe short, suction long, high speed.
Air vessels: reduce acceleration head, make flow uniform, save power (single-acting saves ~84.8%, double-acting ~39.2%).
Other: jet pump, hydraulic ram (uses water hammer), air lift pump, submersible pump.
Hydraulic ram efficiency (D'Aubuisson / Rankine). Hydraulic press, accumulator, intensifier, lift, coupling, torque converter: hydraulic devices.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. — Pump H–Q and efficiency curves with system curve and operating point.
Cavitation in pumps: Occurs at impeller eye when suction pressure < vapour pressure; avoided by NPSHa > NPSHr, low suction lift, larger suction pipe.
Selection: Low head, large Q (drainage, irrigation lift) → axial/mixed-flow pumps; high head (tube wells, high-rise) → multistage centrifugal/submersible.
Series: heads add (same Q); parallel: discharges add (same H). Affinity: Q ∝ N, H ∝ N², P ∝ N³.

s.t: More on this topic — Hydraulics: Pumps
b: Centrifugal pump: converts mechanical energy to pressure energy by centrifugal action; high discharge, moderate head.
Priming: filling casing and suction pipe with liquid before start — essential for centrifugal pumps.
Manometric head H_m = head imparted by pump = static head + losses + exit velocity head.
Manometric efficiency = gH_m / (V_w2 u₂). Overall efficiency = ρgQH_m / shaft power.
Minimum starting speed: u₂² − u₁² ≥ 2gH_m (centrifugal head must exceed manometric head).
Specific speed N_s = N√Q / H^(3/4). Radial (low N_s), mixed flow, axial (high N_s).
Vane shape: backward-curved vanes (most common, stable characteristics); forward-curved rarely used.
Casings: volute, vortex (whirlpool chamber), diffuser (guide vanes).
Pumps in series: same Q, heads add (high head). In parallel: same head, discharges add (high flow).
Multistage pump: impellers in series for high head.
NPSH (Net Positive Suction Head): available must exceed required to avoid cavitation.
Affinity laws (same pump): Q ∝ N, H ∝ N², P ∝ N³.
Slip = theoretical − actual discharge; negative slip possible with a long suction pipe, short delivery pipe and high speed.
Air vessels on reciprocating pumps: smooth flow, reduce acceleration head, save power (≈ 84.8% saving in single-acting).
Other machines: hydraulic ram (uses water hammer to lift water), hydraulic press, accumulator, intensifier, jack, crane, torque converter, fluid coupling, jet pump, air-lift pump, gear pump.
Speed of sound C = √(kRT) (gas) or √(K/ρ) (liquid). In air at 20°C ≈ 343 m/s; in water ≈ 1480 m/s.
Choked flow: max discharge through nozzle when throat M = 1.
Subsonic: diverging section decelerates flow. Supersonic: diverging section accelerates flow (De Laval nozzle).
Normal shock: supersonic → subsonic; irreversible; entropy increases.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
In supersonic flow a diverging passage ACCELERATES the flow (opposite of subsonic) — principle of the convergent-divergent (de Laval) nozzle.
